results.title: Comparative Analysis of Iterative Prompt Refinement and Quality of LLM-Generated Code: Human Evaluation Still Essential
results.abstract: Code generation has become a crucial component of software development, facilitating the rapid and automatic generation of source code from human prompts. Studies providing multi-dimensional performance analyses across models and programming tasks remain scarce, notwithstanding the software engineering community's need for insights into the utility of code generation algorithms. This study investigates the behaviour of large language models (LLMs) under iterative prompt refinement when generating widely used JavaScript code. We evaluate three models (GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Opus 4) across 30 programming tasks, spanning three task types: data structures and algorithms, object-oriented programming (OOP), and web development. The quality of the generated code is assessed along four dimensions: correctness, maintainability, security, and manual evaluation. We found that iterative refinement does not produce consistent improvements across models. Claude exhibits a gradual decline in correctness, GPT-4.1 experiences diminishing returns after the initial refinement, and Gemini 2.5 Pro follows a dip-and-recovery pattern. Maintainability and security remain consistently high across iterations, resulting in overall quality being driven primarily by correctness. Correlations between iteration-to-iteration changes across quality dimensions are generally weak, while task type seems to influence model performance. Further, human evaluation revealed that code judged to be correct, maintainable, and secure was not always considered acceptable, highlighting the importance of assessing aspects of code quality beyond automated metrics. Overall, iterative refinement is neither consistently beneficial nor predictable, correctness provides the most reliable indicator of refinement success, and human evaluation remains indispensable for assessing the practical acceptability of LLM-generated code.

results.title: Security Weaknesses in LLM-Generated Source Code: An Empirical Vulnerability Analysis of Iterative AI-Assisted Development
results.abstract: Context: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineeringworkflows for code generation, debugging, refactoring, and feature development. While previousresearch has examined the security of one-shot code generation, the longitudinal impact of iterativeAI-assisted software refinement on software security remains insufficiently understood.Objective: This study investigates how software vulnerabilities evolve throughout iterative AI-assisted development workflows and introduces a framework for measuring security degradationduring conversational software refinement.Method: We propose SecureIterate, a longitudinal evaluation framework that combines promptorchestration, version tracking, static analysis, runtime validation, fuzz testing, and CWE/OWASP-based vulnerability normalization. Using 1,250 generated software versions spanning multiple pro-gramming languages, application categories, and commercial and open-source LLM families, weevaluate vulnerability propagation across repeated refinement stages. Security Drift Score (SDS) andWeighted Security Drift Score (WSDS) are introduced to quantify longitudinal security changes.Results: The experimental results reveal statistically significant vulnerability growth throughoutiterative refinement cycles. Common weaknesses included SQL injection, improper authentication,hardcoded credentials, path traversal, insecure deserialization, and unsafe dependency usage. Cross-model analysis showed that vulnerability propagation occurred across all evaluated LLM families.Runtime validation and fuzz testing identified additional security issues not detected through staticanalysis alone. Security-aware prompting, static-analysis-guided refinement, and dependency verifi-cation reduced vulnerability growth and improved security outcomes.Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that iterative AI-assisted software development can introducemeasurable security drift despite functional improvements. SecureIterate provides a reproducibleframework for evaluating longitudinal software security and highlights the importance of continuoussecurity validation, automated assurance mechanisms, and human oversight in AI-assisted softwareengineering workflows.

results.title: Evaluating security and inclusivity in LLM-generated code
Auditing Synthetic Code: A Multi-Dimensional Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework for LLM-Generated Code Training Data
results.abstract: Background: LLM-generated synthetic code is now a standard ingredient in code-LM training, but its quality is rarely audited before entering the fine-tune loop. The de facto n-gram contamination check over-flags universal boilerplate and under-flags problem-level paraphrase, and the literature lacks a structured measurement scaffold to take its place.Methods: We propose an audit taxonomy with operational framework for LLM-generated synthetic code, mapped to ISO/IEC 25010 software-quality characteristics. The taxonomy organises nine dimensions into three operational bands (contamination, structural-and-semantic, execution), embeds a rule-based two-axis contamination diagnostic with four operationally distinct cells, and is exposed through a deterministic open-source Python implementation. We apply the audit taxonomy to five public synthetic-code datasets and validate it downstream by LoRA-fine-tuning code-LMs across three Qwen-Coder sizes, StarCoder2-3B, and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B on MBPP-500 and HumanEval.Results: Four strong-signal axes discriminate the datasets at medium-to-large multi-seed effect sizes (Friedman p <= 0.0012 on every strong axis). A uniform-weight five-axis composite rank-orders the five datasets against MBPP-500 pass@1 within the Qwen-Coder family (Spearman rho >= +0.70); cross-family transfer is partial on StarCoder2-3B (rho = +0.60) and does not hold on DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B (rho = -0.20). HumanEval inverts the ordering, showing benchmark-contingent predictivity.Conclusions: The audit taxonomy discriminates synthetic-code datasets consistently and supplies a reusable knowledge artefact for synthetic-data quality assurance. Downstream predictivity is family- and benchmark-contingent; we report it as bounded validation evidence rather than a general predictivity claim.

results.title: Evaluating Security and Inclusivity in LLM-Generated Code: A Controlled Experiment
results.abstract: Despite developments in the human aspects of cybersecurity, inclusivity concerns, particularly related to neurodiversity, remain largely unexplored. One reason for this gap is a limited understanding among practitioners concerning inclusivity and neurodiversity. This paper examines the role that Large Language Models (LLMs) can play in generating code that integrates inclusivity concerns in the development of security systems and services. A controlled experiment was conducted with three experimental cases, constructed by varying the level of inclusivity specification from no specification in the first case to a detailed specification in the third. Moreover, after each round, the LLM-generated code artifact was evaluated against security and inclusivity criteria by 13 human experts and five LLM-based reviewers using a rubric-based assessment. The results demonstrate that an increase in the specification detail improves the inclusivity of LLM-generated code without causing any negative impact (trade-offs) on security. Statistical comparisons using Welch’s independentsamples t-tests revealed no statistically significant difference between human and LLM-based evaluations for inclusivity, whereas a significant difference was observed for security assessments. Effect size analysis (Cohen’s d) indicated a substantial divergence in security evaluation patterns between humans and LLM evaluators. The findings have implications for (i) research in terms of advancing the state of the art concerning integration of LLMs in the phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC), secure software engineering, and (ii) practice in terms of the role of specification details, and complementary strengths between human and LLM evaluators to support evaluation of LLM-generated code.
